name: Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi
powers: Said to command the wind and fell whole fields of grass; one of the Three Sacred Treasures.
description: The legendary grass-cutting sword drawn from the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi by the storm god Susanoo, who then offered it to his sister Amaterasu; it is the sword of the Three Sacred Treasures of the Japanese imperial regalia, with the mirror and the jewel. Its name, 'grass-cutter', recalls the later story of the hero Yamato Takeru, who escaped a burning field by using the blade to mow the grass and turn the fire back on his enemies. The sword is said to be kept at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, where it is guarded and almost never shown, and no one outside the shrine has verified its state. Alongside the mirror and the jewel it stands for the martial virtue of the imperial line and for the divine descent of the throne, as told in the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki.

name: Yata no Kagami
powers: Reflects truth and brilliance; part of the imperial regalia.
description: The Eight-Fold Mirror hung from a sacred sakaki tree outside the rock-cave in which the sun goddess Amaterasu had hidden, its brilliance luring her out to illuminate the world again, in the central myth of Japanese kingship. Revered at Ise Grand Shrine as the mirror of the Three Sacred Treasures, it is held to represent the sun goddess and, with the jewel and the sword, the imperial regalia; its polished face stands for truth and reflection in Shinto thought. The mirror, like the other treasures, is wrapped and kept from public view, so that all descriptions of it rest on the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki rather than on sight. Bronze mirrors from the Yayoi and Kofun periods, found in burials by the hundreds, show how old and how central the sacred mirror was to the culture that gave Amaterasu her tale.

name: Yasakani no Magatama
powers: Symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's right to rule.
description: The curved jade bead (magatama) dangled from the branch of the sacred sakaki tree beside the mirror that drew Amaterasu from her cave, and counted among the Three Sacred Treasures of Japan it symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's mandate to rule. The comma-shaped bead is far older than the myth, appearing in Jomon ornament and by the hundreds in Kofun-period tomb jewellery, where the huge jasper magatama found in the great burial mounds shows how much the form was treasured. The name Yasakani is explained in the chronicles as 'the jewel of Yasaka', a place-name tied to the shrine of Yasaka in Kyoto, though the identification is disputed. Together with the mirror and the sword, the magatama stands for the gentleness of the sovereign, one of the three treasures that together legitimise the imperial throne.

name: Shichishito
description: An iron sword with seven branch-like projections along its blade, dedicated at the Isonokami Shrine in Nara and recorded in the Nihon Shoki as a gift from the kingdom of Baekje to the Yamato court. Its long gold-inlaid inscription, which dates the sword to the mid-fourth century, describes offerings made to a sun deity and names the Baekje court that sent it, making it one of the oldest inscribed iron objects of Japan and a rare physical relic of early Korean-Japanese exchange. With its strange branched form it is not a practical weapon, and it is best understood as a ritual or ceremonial sword, kept for centuries as a shrine treasure. Today it is registered as a National Treasure of Japan and displayed only rarely, still guarded at the shrine that received it some sixteen hundred years ago.

name: Hannya Mask
powers: Embodies a woman turned demon by jealousy
description: The hannya is a Noh theatre mask sculpted as the face of a woman transfigured by jealousy, resentment, or obsessive love into a horned, serpent-eyed demon with a gaping, fang-filled mouth and trailing metallic teeth. It is worn in plays such as Dojoji, where a spurned woman becomes a serpent that pursues the monk Anchin into a temple bell, and Aoi no Ue, where the living Rokujo no Miyasudokoro torments her rival through spirit-doctoring. The mask is carved in ascending grades of intensity, from a slightly raised mouth to a fully open jaw with gilded fangs, so a single hannya can move on stage from grief to pure fury. In the folk tradition the finished mask is treated with care because it is thought to retain the dangerous emotional charge it depicts, and carvers historically disposed of flawed examples ritually rather than letting them circulate. The hannya name is also used for the demon itself in the wider yokai lore that grew up around the Noh stage.

name: Oni no Kanabo
powers: Said to crush any demon or mortal it strikes
description: The kanabo is the iron-studded club that Japanese legend and art place in the grip of the oni, the ogre of the folk imagination, and it has become the oni's stock attribute to the point that the two are nearly inseparable in picture scrolls and festival prints. Tales from the Heian-era exploits of the demon queller Minamoto no Yorimitsu, above all his campaign against the bandit-ogre Shuten-doji, show the oni swinging the heavy mace with crushing force against heroes and their retainers; the same weapon appears in the folk tale of Momotaro, whose companions win against the ogres' island through wit. The club is conventionally imagined as a wooden shaft bound with iron hoops and studded with iron knobs, heavier than a man could lift, and it is treated as a mythological attribute rather than a documented artifact, since no original example survives. It carries real cultural weight, standing for brute strength that must be overcome by cleverness, and it remains the default prop of oni in the Setsubun bean-throwing rite and in modern manga and games.

name: Shimenawa
powers: Marks off divine ground and repels impurity
description: The shimenawa is the sacred rope twisted from rice straw that marks off the dwelling-place of the kami in Shinto practice, hung across the entrance of shrines, over torii gates, and around sacred trees, rocks, and rice paddies. Its origin is tied to the founding myth of the sun goddess Amaterasu, who sealed herself in the Heavenly Rock Cave and left the world in darkness until the other gods lured her out and strung a rope across the mouth of the cave to keep her from retreating again. The shimenawa draws a boundary between the purified ground of the kami and the defiling world outside, and its presence warns humans not to cross unbidden. It is braided from freshly harvested straw, in some regions hemp or straw hung with the paper streamers called shide, and the rope is renewed each year as part of New Year preparations at shrines across Japan. Larger examples, some spanning several metres, hang over the great torii of shrines such as Izumo Taisha and Fushimi Inari, making the rope one of the most visible symbols of Shinto itself.

name: Hagoromo
powers: Lets its wearer fly between heaven and earth
description: Hagoromo, the feather mantle, is the robe that lets a heavenly maiden, the tennyo, fly between the mortal world and the sky, and it is the central object of one of the most famous Noh plays, Hagoromo, set at Mio Bay. In the play a fisherman named Hakuryo finds a robe of feathers hanging from a pine and refuses to return it until the angel who owns it teaches him the dance of the moon palace, the promise of the robe's return drawing the divine world briefly into the human. The story belongs to the wider family of swan-maiden tales told across Eurasia, in which a supernatural woman loses her flying garment, marries a mortal, and departs when the garment is restored. In Japanese folklore the robe is woven from a thousand feathers and cannot be lifted by any ordinary hand, and a man who hides it may win the maiden's love but loses her when it is found. The play's theme of the boundary between human and divine, and the price of crossing it, has made the hagoromo a staple of Japanese literature and a name given to shrines and dance traditions honouring the heavenly maidens.
source: Noh play Hagoromo; coastal legend tradition

name: Kitsune's Crescent Comb
powers: Reveals a fox in human form; granting it service or love
description: The crescent-shaped comb of Japanese legend is the small hair ornament that a shapeshifting kitsune is said to drop when its disguise is betrayed, and finding it is supposed to bring a strange fortune or a lasting bond with the fox. The comb appears again and again in tales of fox wives, in which a man marries a beautiful woman who turns out to be a fox in human form; at the crucial moment the tail is seen, or the comb is left behind when the wife vanishes, and the discovery ends the marriage. In some variants the man who keeps the comb may command the fox's service or its gratitude, while in others the comb proves the spirit nature of the householder and drives the fox away for good. Because the fox in Japanese belief is both a trickster and a messenger of the rice god Inari, the comb carries an ambiguous charge: it is a clue, a keepsake, and a token of a crossing between the animal and human worlds. The motif is old enough to appear in the earliest collections of Japanese fox tales, and it still shapes modern retellings in which a comb on a shrine step promises a fox encounter.

name: Daruma Doll
powers: Talisman of perseverance and wish fulfillment
description: The daruma is a rounded paper-mache doll modelled on Bodhidharma, the semi-legendary founder of Zen Buddhism, whose hollow weighted body always rocks back upright when tipped. The likeness plays on a famous story in which Bodhidharma sat facing a wall in meditation for nine years, until his legs withered and were lost; the doll keeps his determined, round form and his fierce brow. Bought as a talisman of perseverance, the daruma is customarily sold with blank white eyes, and the owner inks in one eye when a wish or goal is set and the second when it is achieved, the rite turning the doll into a kind of visual contract with oneself. At the end of the year the accumulated daruma are taken to temples such as Dairyoji in Gunma, the dolls' birthplace, and burned in the daruma-kuyo ceremony, releasing the accumulated wishes. Originally a charm against smallpox in the Edo period, the doll has become a national symbol of resilience, famously adopted by political candidates, and its self-righting property gives the Japanese phrase 'falling seven times, rising eight' a concrete image.
